title: The Gang Goes Bowling

jokes.text: They'll be mush by the time they get here. No way.
jokes.setup: Someone wants to order chili cheese fries for delivery to the bar
jokes.punchline: Dennis dismisses it with practical logic — a mundane, grounded refusal in a show about chaos
jokes.explanation: Mildly amusing cold-open gag. Practical logic as anti-humor in a show known for chaos. Weak setup with no real payoff — functions mainly as scene-setting.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: A delivery of chili cheese fries? They'll be mush by the time they get here. No way.

jokes.text: Well, finesse isn't really my style, Charlie. I like to dominate the table into submission.
jokes.setup: Charlie tells Dennis he needs more finesse playing something at the bar
jokes.punchline: Dennis reframes aggressive domination as a legitimate style choice, with disturbing earnestness
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis characterization — his pathological need for dominance applied even to casual games. The phrase 'dominate the table into submission' is well-constructed and very on-brand. Sets up finesse as a running gag for the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Well, finesse isn't really my style, Charlie. I like to dominate the table into submission.

jokes.text: It's 'cause you're sneaking around trying to steal money that you haven't earned and looking like Carmen Sandiego.
jokes.setup: Dee is wearing a long coat and trying to get money from the register without explanation
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a layered insult — calling out her theft AND her fashion sense in one breath with the Carmen Sandiego reference
jokes.explanation: Sharp, specific insult. Carmen Sandiego is an unexpected but apt reference — mysterious coat, sneaking around. The layered accusation (stealing + fashion) is economical and very Dennis. Good laugh line.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: looking like Carmen Sandiego

jokes.text: Dee dramatically reveals she's wearing a bowling shirt under her coat — she was hiding that she was going bowling
jokes.setup: Everyone suspects Dee is hiding something scandalous under her coat; Mac tries to rip it off her
jokes.punchline: The big reveal is merely a bowling shirt — the entire confrontation was over something completely mundane
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny escalation-to-nothing structure. The gang's paranoid interrogation is played like a thriller; the payoff is a bowling shirt. Well-structured anticlimax with a good visual beat and a 5-second pause before the reveal.

dialogue.line: Visual gag: Dee reveals bowling shirt under coat after dramatic buildup

jokes.text: As if. As if, Dee. As if. As if. As if, Dee. As if.
jokes.setup: Dee explains she doesn't want the gang involved in her bowling because it's her thing
jokes.punchline: All four gang members simultaneously echo 'as if' in a synchronized dismissal — the comedic effect is in the repetition and unanimity
jokes.explanation: The humor is in the chorus of dismissal — four voices piling on creates a mob mentality joke. The '90s slang 'as if' is funny coming from these middle-aged men. Slight, but lands as a quick laugh.

dialogue.line: As if. As if, Dee. As if. As if. As if, Dee. As if.

jokes.text: Ding-dongs in our hand... What is she talking... My ding-dong wasn't even in my hand. Mine was. Yeah, so was mine. Yeah, I was scratching mine when she said that. I had my hands fully down my pants, if I'm being honest. I had to push it to the left.
jokes.setup: Dee dismissively tells the guys to enjoy sitting around with their 'ding-dongs in their hands'
jokes.punchline: Each man in turn admits they literally had their hands on/in their pants — escalating from denial to full confession, with Frank's 'push it to the left' as the capper
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation structure — starts with plausible denial, each admission gets more specific and gross, culminating in Frank's matter-of-fact anatomical precision. The structure mirrors classic Sunny ensemble comedy where the gang inadvertently confirms the worst about themselves. 'Push it to the left' is an excellent topper. Each character's response fits their established personality.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: My ding-dong wasn't even in my hand. I mean, what do you...

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Mine was.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, so was mine.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, I was scratching mine when she said that.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I-I had my hands fully down my pants, if I'm being honest. I had to push it to the left.

jokes.text: Well, I'm gonna head out. You guys enjoy sitting around with your ding-dongs in your hand doing nothing all night.
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to make a dignified exit after being mocked.
jokes.punchline: Her parting shot accidentally (or maybe intentionally) describes the guys literally holding their penises.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the funnier joke that follows. On its own, it's a decent enough exit line from Dee, but it exists primarily to enable the gang's response.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, hello, ladies. You ready to roll?

jokes.text: It was a lucky guess. That's a crazy... yeah. It was a lucky guess.
jokes.setup: The gang has just admitted they all had their hands on their genitals when Dee said 'ding-dongs in your hand'
jokes.punchline: They rationalize Dee's accurate assessment as a 'lucky guess' rather than acknowledging the obvious truth
jokes.explanation: Good button on the previous joke — the gang's self-deception is a core character trait and this coda reinforces it cleanly. Slightly loses steam as the ding-dong bit's energy fades.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: It's just that our fourth didn't show up and literally no one else was free on a Friday night.

jokes.text: ...we have a lot better things to do than just go bowling.
jokes.setup: Dennis has just delivered a speech about how they have better things to do
jokes.punchline: Cut immediately to the gang arriving at the bowling alley — they had nothing better to do
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom cut — character insists they won't do the thing, immediate cut to them doing the thing. Well-executed structural joke. The gap between Dennis's self-important declaration and reality is very Sunny.

dialogue.speaker: Snail
dialogue.line: I sucked off a rando in the parking lot. Ugh, my mouth hurts.

jokes.text: It's just that our fourth didn't show up and literally no one else was free on a Friday night.
jokes.setup: Dee arrives late and announces she shows up when she wants as a power move
jokes.punchline: The Waitress deflates her entirely — Dee wasn't wanted, she was the last resort
jokes.explanation: Clean deflation of Dee's delusion. The specificity of 'literally no one else was free on a Friday night' is nicely brutal. Dee as the loser of last resort is a recurring dynamic that works here.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Frige-it Bitches

jokes.text: Anyone want to snort Jell-O shots? ...Snail? You're on the team? Yeah, I love bowling. The whole scene is so hot. I sucked off a rando in the parking lot. Ugh, my mouth hurts.
jokes.setup: Dee's bowling team is introduced; a new character named 'Snail' arrives
jokes.punchline: Snail immediately establishes herself as aggressively sexual and unhinged — sucking off a stranger in the parking lot before a bowling league match, delivered with complete casualness
jokes.explanation: Snail is an effective one-joke character — the joke is her complete lack of filter or shame. 'My mouth hurts' as the capper is a good economy beat. Slightly cheap (shock value), but executed with enough specificity to work.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Or perhaps I should let my balls do the talking.

jokes.text: Your cooter is most likely on fire from a yeast infection. Go in the bathroom, rinse it out and be better next time.
jokes.setup: Snail announces her 'cooter's on fire for Mac' after his roll
jokes.punchline: Dee responds not with disgust but with a clinical medical diagnosis and a practical solution delivered as sports coaching
jokes.explanation: Brilliant tone blend — clinical medical language delivered as sports coaching. 'Be better next time' as the button is perfect. The joke works on multiple levels: Dee's obliviousness to social norms, the absurdity of treating a yeast infection as a performance issue, and the economy of the construction. Genuinely sharp writing.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Vaginas and penises together again.

jokes.text: Or perhaps I should let my balls do the talking.
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to establish herself as team leader and expert bowler
jokes.punchline: Accidental double entendre — 'balls' referring to bowling balls but landing as sexual innuendo
jokes.explanation: Generic double-entendre. It lands because of the bowling context but isn't particularly clever. The 'Please do / Yeah' response suggests the other characters also hear the double meaning, which saves it slightly, but this is a well-worn joke template.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: He did one, so I thought we were doing... Okay.

jokes.text: So these 'frigid bitches' — these are your new 'fancy friends'? What is this, some kind of women's league? Vaginas and penises together again.
jokes.setup: Dennis arrives to mock Dee's 'fancy outing' which turned out to be bowling
jokes.punchline: 'Vaginas and penises together again' — Dennis summarizing a coed tournament with the most reductive, clinical, and weirdly poetic framing possible
jokes.explanation: Very Dennis — his pseudo-intellectual reduction of a coed tournament to anatomy is both revealing of his character and genuinely funny. 'Together again' implies a failed reunion, adding an absurd undertone. Good character-specific line.

dialogue.speaker: Liam
dialogue.line: Ryan's got the forearms of an elephant wrangler. He could have been pro. I could have been. If not for my tragic accident.

jokes.text: He did one, so I thought we were doing... Okay. / Anyone got a straw?
jokes.setup: Mac does a dramatic challenge pose; Charlie interprets it as a signal to do something
jokes.punchline: Charlie has apparently snorted a Jell-O shot and is now asking for a straw — visual comedy of Charlie just doing things impulsively
jokes.explanation: Charlie being Charlie — impulsive, context-free, committed. The logic 'he did one so I thought we were doing' is perfect Charlie reasoning. Mid-tier but solid character moment.

dialogue.line: The story is too horrible for words, so don't ask me...

jokes.text: We got out of the video rental business just after the bubble burst. Bowling's always been in our blood. Ryan's got the forearms of an elephant wrangler. He could have been pro. I could have. If not for my tragic accident. The story is too horrible for words, so don't ask me...
jokes.setup: The McPoyle brothers unexpectedly own the bowling alley
jokes.punchline: Liam builds to a 'tragic accident' backstory with maximum dramatic gravitas, insisting the story is too horrible to tell — which the gang immediately and completely ignores
jokes.explanation: The McPoyles are perfectly deployed here. 'Forearms of an elephant wrangler' is a vivid, absurd compliment. The 'tragic accident' setup is an extended misdirect — the audience expects a horror story but won't get it until much later. The gang's immediate dismissal ('We don't want to hear it' / 'You clearly want to tell us') is a great dynamic. Rewatch bonus because the payoff (a pinched finger) recontextualizes all this gravitas hilariously.

dialogue.line: combining them is strictly prohibited... The story is too terrible to tell.

jokes.text: Franklin, we do have chili and we do have cheese and we do have fries, but combining them is strictly prohibited. The story is too terrible to tell.
jokes.setup: Frank asks if the bowling alley has chili cheese fries
jokes.punchline: Liam mirrors his own 'story too horrible to tell' construction but applies it to a food combination — a perfect absurdist echo
jokes.explanation: Exceptional callback structure. Liam's 'story too horrible to tell' construction is immediately repurposed for the mundane topic of chili cheese fries, which both expands the joke's universe and sets up another misdirect. The parallel construction ('we do have chili AND cheese AND fries but...') is meticulous setup work. The payoff (chili cheese fries caused the bowling accident) hasn't landed yet, making this a great plant. Near-exceptional comedic writing for a minor character bit.

dialogue.line: Hanging Monster Dong Lucky Strike Chili Cheese Fryers

jokes.text: Oh, it looks huge. Sick. Can we take another? I wasn't sufficiently in character.
jokes.setup: The gang takes a team photo; Artemis checks the picture
jokes.punchline: Artemis is delighted her ass looks huge in the photo, then requests a retake because she 'wasn't sufficiently in character'
jokes.explanation: Two-beat joke: the delight at her ass looking huge (self-absorbed Artemis) followed by the pivot to 'in character' (the acting delusion). Both beats work, and together they're a good Artemis character capsule.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: It's too many ideas, man. I told you it was stupid. I-I knew they were gonna make fun of us and they did make fun of us.

jokes.text: I'm researching a character I'm playing named Donna Brunswick of the Brunswick Bowling Dynasty.
jokes.setup: Artemis is at a casual bowling league match
jokes.punchline: She has invented an elaborate fictional character with dynastic bowling lineage for a recreational league — complete method acting commitment for a completely inappropriate context
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Artemis. The specificity of 'Brunswick Bowling Dynasty' (a real bowling brand, making it funnier) and her total commitment to this fictional persona for a meaningless league is excellent character comedy. The name 'Donna Brunswick' is a great invention. This pays off when Donna bowls a strike and when Artemis takes a 'quickie' mid-match for her character.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Now, I'm no fan of women's sports. Who is? Yeah, they're not very popular. Nobody is. Nobody watches... Especially women. Women don't even like women's sports.

jokes.text: Oh, goddamn. You guys are not taking this seriously. Okay? Let's cut the BS. As your leader, I demand we cut the BS.
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to run her bowling team with authority
jokes.punchline: Dee's attempt at serious leadership is undercut by the absurdity of demanding people cut BS while standing in a bowling alley with a team called 'Frige-it Bitches'
jokes.explanation: Functional Dee delusion joke — she thinks she's a serious leader. Mid-tier; the specific lines aren't that sharp but the character beat is consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Stride, stride, stride, execute.

jokes.text: Well, well, well. Looks like the Frigid Bitches are going up against the Hanging Monster Dong Lucky Strike Chili Cheese Fryers.
jokes.setup: The bracket pairs the women's team against the guys' team. The guys' team name has been a running discussion.
jokes.punchline: The full team name — 'Hanging Monster Dong Lucky Strike Chili Cheese Fryers' — announced by Liam McPoyle all at once, reveals the absurd over-stuffed compromise the guys reached.
jokes.explanation: The reveal of the full team name is a great comedic moment — it's so overcrowded that it proves the gang couldn't agree on anything and just kept adding to it. The juxtaposition with 'Frigid Bitches' (clean, simple, funny) makes the guys look even more ridiculous. The McPoyle deadpan delivery adds to it.

dialogue.speaker: Snail
dialogue.line: Ooh, my cooter's on fire for Mac.

jokes.text: I'm thinking Snail, Artemis, Waitress, best for last.
jokes.setup: Dee announces the batting order
jokes.punchline: Waitress points out Dee doesn't even know everyone's names — undercutting her 'leader' claim
jokes.explanation: Minor joke — the irony of Dee as a leader who doesn't know her team members' names works as a quick beat. Functional but not memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Your cooter is most likely on fire from a yeast infection. Go in the bathroom, rinse it out and be better next time.

jokes.text: The gang's team name is revealed: 'Hanging Monster Dong Lucky Strike Chili Cheese Fryers'
jokes.setup: Team names are announced before the match
jokes.punchline: The gang's team name is a ridiculous amalgam of too many ideas — 'Hanging Monster Dong' (intimidation) + 'Lucky Strike' (bowling reference) + 'Chili Cheese Fryers' (the opening gag) — none of which go together
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the excess — too many concepts forced together. 'I told you it was stupid' and 'it's too many ideas' as the gang's own self-critique is perfectly self-aware. The callback to chili cheese fries elevates it. The admission 'I knew they were gonna make fun of us and they did' is a great beat.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: My character can. Me, I can't bowl for shit.

jokes.text: Now, I'm no fan of women's sports. Who is? Yeah, they're not very popular. Nobody is. Nobody watches... Especially women. Women don't even like women's sports.
jokes.setup: Dennis is telling the story of young Dee captaining the girls' bowling team
jokes.punchline: The whole gang piles on with casual misogynistic dismissal of women's sports, including the observation that 'women don't even like women's sports' — delivered as shared wisdom
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny gang-thinks ensemble moment. The escalating agreement is funny, and the self-negating logic of 'women don't even like women's sports' is sharp. The joke's intent is to expose the gang's casual sexism as the butt, which is the show's standard approach.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Frank celebrates getting a strike by slowly crawling under pins

jokes.text: And to prove that Dee's female mind was mentally weak, I started to go watch her, and I would say 'gutter ball' right before she rolled it, and wouldn't you know it, every time I said it, she'd roll a gutter ball.
jokes.setup: Dennis is narrating how he psychologically sabotaged young Dee's bowling career
jokes.punchline: He conditioned her to roll gutter balls through psychological abuse, framing it as a scientific experiment to prove women are 'mentally weak' — delivered with complete self-satisfaction
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and core to the Dennis character. The specificity of Dennis's cruelty — deliberately conditioning his sister through psychological warfare, framing it as a scientific proof — is peak Dennis Reynolds. The casual pride in describing childhood emotional abuse as an experiment is deeply dark and deeply funny. The structure is excellent: the setup builds with apparent pride, the act itself is horrifying, and the payoff (he still does it) drives the entire third act. Character integration is a 9 because only Dennis would do this AND tell people about it proudly. This is what the show does best.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: A quickie. Quickie it is. My character is also a giant whore, which is what attracted me to the role in the first place, so...

jokes.text: Well, that's a bit of an exaggeration. / Anyway, good luck out there.
jokes.setup: Dennis has just told everyone that Dee can't knock down a single pin when he looks at her
jokes.punchline: Dee's only response is a meek 'that's a bit of an exaggeration' — not a denial — before Dennis cheerfully waves them off. Her weak protest confirms the story is basically true.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the gutter ball setup. Dee's feeble non-denial ('a bit of an exaggeration') is funnier than outright refusal — it implies the story is mostly true. Dennis's breezy 'Anyway, good luck out there' as if he hasn't just described childhood psychological warfare is a great character beat. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Hey, Tyrone, do not take my spot! Do not take my spot at the air hockey table.

jokes.text: Anyway, good luck out there. / Mm. / Ladies. / Gentlemen. / That was so good. / That was really good. / That was really good, Dennis.
jokes.setup: Dennis finishes telling the story designed to psychologically harm Dee before the match.
jokes.punchline: The guys congratulate Dennis on the story — 'that was really good, Dennis' — as if he just performed something impressive rather than recounted deliberate psychological abuse of their friend.
jokes.explanation: Good button on the Dennis story. The guys treating psychological abuse like a performance worth complimenting is classically in-character for the group. 'That was really good, Dennis' in particular sounds like praise for a good bit at a comedy show.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: By the way, your hair looks great.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Charlie, shut up, I'm trying to focus.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Did you, like, change your hair or something?

jokes.text: Oh, shit. What? Some kid's having, like, a birthday party in the arcade or something. Okay. So what? It looks fun.
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to organize the team's bowling strategy
jokes.punchline: Charlie is immediately distracted by a child's birthday party in the arcade — suggesting he finds a kids' party more appealing than the actual competition
jokes.explanation: Setup for the Charlie birthday party running gag. Charlie's childlike wonder at a kids' party is consistent characterization. Mid-tier on its own but serves as important setup.

dialogue.line: Gutter ball.

jokes.text: Charlie, do not be that guy that everyone's looking for when it's their turn. That shit drives me crazy.
jokes.setup: Charlie wants to go to the arcade party instead of bowling.
jokes.punchline: Mac's very specific, earnest warning about bowling etiquette is funny because (a) Mac is not someone who typically cares about etiquette, and (b) it's completely useless — Charlie will absolutely be that guy.
jokes.explanation: Decent setup for the inevitable payoff when Charlie repeatedly disappears. Mac's sincerity about bowling etiquette is mildly funny given his usual moral code.

dialogue.line: Gutter ball.

jokes.text: Stride, stride, stride, execute.
jokes.setup: Mac approaches the lane to bowl
jokes.punchline: Mac narrates his own approach in sports-movie internal monologue style — 'stride, stride, stride, execute' — as if he's narrating a highlight reel of his own athletic prowess
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — four words that perfectly capture Mac's obsession with his own athletic image and his tendency to narrate himself heroically. The rhythm of 'stride, stride, stride' as a chant before bowling is both specific and absurd. Becomes a callback later when Mac fails. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Besides your physical limitations, if given the opportunity to either work together as a team or tear each other apart, you will always choose the latter. Because women are devious and destructive and will always default to using their insidious venom on the most sought-after victim of all... each other.

jokes.text: Ooh, my cooter's on fire for Mac. I want to have his baby.
jokes.setup: Mac bowls a decent shot
jokes.punchline: Snail immediately announces sexual desire for Mac in the most graphic terms
jokes.explanation: Consistent Snail characterization. Less fresh than her introduction since we now know her deal. The yeast infection callback elevates it, but on its own it's repetitive.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Because... they're stupid.

jokes.text: Dennis, cover me. Cover me. / I can't do that right now. / What? Just go, go... / No, I got... / Go stand over here. / I got Liam over here eyeballing me. / I mean... I think he is. Little hard to tell with the eyepatch.
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to do something illicit (mix substances) while being watched
jokes.punchline: Dennis can't help because he too is being watched by a McPoyle — then undercuts the tension by noting 'little hard to tell with the eyepatch'
jokes.explanation: Good beat — the McPoyles as surveillance figures is consistent with their creepiness. 'Hard to tell with the eyepatch' is a solid topper that gets a laugh from deadpan observation about a disability in a completely inappropriate context, which is Sunny's wheelhouse.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Don't-don't do it. Don't do it. Just play your game.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Can I just spin one? I don't care... Let me spin one.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You don't need to spin it. You just play your game and we're gonna win. Okay? Do not spin it. Do not do it.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. I won't, I won't spin it. I won't.

jokes.text: Frank propositions Artemis for 'the back seat of my LeBaron after the roll'
jokes.setup: It's Artemis's turn to bowl
jokes.punchline: Frank makes a romantic/sexual proposition in the middle of a competitive bowling match, citing the specificity of 'my LeBaron'
jokes.explanation: Frank's LeBaron is a recurring detail that makes his sleaziness funnier through specificity. The timing (mid-competition) adds to the absurdity. Functional Frank/Artemis dynamic joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Stride, stride, stride, spin!

jokes.text: Everybody stop trying to have sex with each other.
jokes.setup: Frank propositions Artemis; Snail has been announcing her desire for Mac
jokes.punchline: Dee addresses the entire situation with one blanket command — 'everybody stop trying to have sex with each other' — as if this is a normal coaching note
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — a single line that recontextualizes the chaos of the last few minutes as a coherent problem to be solved. Dee as the exasperated straight man here is funny precisely because she's usually the most chaos-adjacent character. Very clean construction.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Hey, Tyrone, double or nothing! 'Cause there's no way you're beating me two out of three, dude!

jokes.text: Strike. / Artemis, you can bowl? / No. My character can. Me, I can't bowl for shit.
jokes.setup: Artemis in full 'Donna Brunswick' character rolls a strike
jokes.punchline: Artemis clarifies that SHE can't bowl — only her character Donna can. The method acting is so complete it has physically manifested
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The payoff to the Donna Brunswick setup is extraordinary — the logical absurdity that method acting could genuinely produce physical skills that the actor doesn't have is both a perfect character joke AND a perfect absurdist concept. 'Me, I can't bowl for shit' is an all-time Artemis line. The delivery is everything. This is the kind of joke that makes IASIP great: it commits fully to its own ridiculous premise. High rewatch value because you need to know the setup to appreciate it.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: In the third act of my play, Donna rolls a gutter ball in the big match against her rival high school.

jokes.text: Oh, bullshit. / No, come on, that doesn't count. / Uh, no, the computer counted it, so it counts. / That counts.
jokes.setup: Frank's impossibly slow ball somehow results in a strike.
jokes.punchline: Dee protests it shouldn't count — but 'the computer counted it, so it counts' is the perfect rebuttal that acknowledges the absurdity while upholding the result.
jokes.explanation: Decent follow-up to the Frank strike. 'The computer counted it' is a funny defense of a ridiculous outcome.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: She's a terrible person. She's a bitch and she's ugly and I didn't want her on the team. And she's gross. Sure, and she's gross. But you know what? You're even worse.

jokes.text: Hey, Artemis, let's mush. / A quickie. / Quickie it is. / My character is also a giant whore, which is what attracted me to the role in the first place.
jokes.setup: Frank tries to get Artemis to leave with him mid-match
jokes.punchline: Artemis agrees to a 'quickie' and frames it as method acting — her character is 'a giant whore, which is what attracted me to the role'
jokes.explanation: Excellent Artemis character moment. The method acting conceit reaches its logical extreme — she's not having sex, her CHARACTER is. 'What attracted me to the role in the first place' is a perfect actor-speak line applied to a grotesque situation. This is a 8 on character integration because only Artemis (and only on this show) would rationalize casual sex during a bowling tournament as artistic dedication.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I summon the very fact that I am a man!

jokes.text: Hey, Tyrone, do not take my spot! Do not take my spot at the air hockey table.
jokes.setup: Charlie has wandered off to the birthday party arcade; it's now his turn to bowl
jokes.punchline: Charlie is so embedded in a child's birthday party that he's defending his air hockey spot from a kid named Tyrone
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie moment — his childlike id leads him to fully participate in a child's birthday party, to the point of having an ongoing air hockey rivalry with 'Tyrone.' The specificity of a named child opponent makes this funnier. Excellent character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I've broken every single bone in my hand. I cannot bowl. There's nothing solid left in there. It's just bloody soup and bone broth.

jokes.text: By the way, your hair looks great. / Charlie, shut up, I'm trying to focus. / Did you, like, change your hair or something?
jokes.setup: Charlie finally bowls; Dee is trying to focus on her own mental game
jokes.punchline: Charlie distracts Dee with a sincere, mid-roll compliment about her hair — a completely incongruous moment of sweetness that disrupts her concentration
jokes.explanation: Charlie being obliviously sweet in a competitive context is a good character beat. The sincerity of the compliment is funnier than any deliberate sabotage would be — he's not doing it to be mean, he genuinely noticed her hair. This is a good use of Charlie's specific brand of off-beat social timing.

dialogue.speaker: Ryan
dialogue.line: It pinched it really bad. I had a nasty bruise for a week.

jokes.text: Dennis approaches the lane and says 'I swear to God' he won't say it — then immediately says 'Gutter ball' the moment Dee releases
jokes.setup: Dee confronts Dennis; he swears he won't invoke the curse word
jokes.punchline: He cannot resist — says 'Gutter ball' the moment she releases, and she rolls a gutter ball. First execution of the conditioned response.
jokes.explanation: The long-setup payoff lands perfectly. Dennis promising to behave and immediately breaking his word is character-perfect, and the fact that IT WORKS — Dee actually rolls the gutter ball — validates everything Dennis said earlier. The audience has been waiting for this since the childhood story. The structure is immaculate: setup 7 minutes ago, buildup of trust, instant betrayal, confirmed result. This is excellent sitcom architecture.

jokes.text: Gutter ball. / You-you dick. / Sorry. I'm sorry. / That's not funny. / I couldn't resist. It's... Sorry.
jokes.setup: Dennis promised not to say 'gutter ball' and Dee almost believed him.
jokes.punchline: He immediately says 'gutter ball' just before she rolls — she gets a gutter ball — and then feigns apologetic embarrassment while clearly delighted.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of Dennis's elaborate innocent act — he immediately breaks his promise. The structure is excellent: extreme reassurance → betrayal → fake guilt. 'I couldn't resist. It's... Sorry.' is Dennis's tell — he's not actually sorry at all, and the mid-sentence pause before 'sorry' perfectly captures that. 'I couldn't resist' reads as pure delight.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, hi, Dee. I'm in here, too. Gutter ball.

jokes.text: Second gutter ball — Dennis says it again: 'Gutter ball.' 'You goddamned son of a bitch!'
jokes.setup: Dee's first ball was a gutter ball; she warns Dennis not to do it again
jokes.punchline: He says it again. It works again. Dee's escalating rage is the comedic reward.
jokes.explanation: Second execution of the gag is slightly less fresh but Dee's escalating fury ('You goddamned son of a bitch!') earns it. The repetition is intentional and the audience is now fully invested in this dynamic. The payoff of Dee's specific cursing is good.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh, hi, Dee. I'm in here, too. Gutter ball.

jokes.text: Get off my back, you frigid bitch. / I knew inviting you was a bad idea. / Well, then, don't invite me. Then don't invite me next time. / I didn't invite...
jokes.setup: Dee and the Waitress argue after the gutter ball incident; their team is falling apart
jokes.punchline: The Waitress calls Dee a 'frigid bitch' — the team's own sponsor name has become an insult — and they bicker about invitations, with Dee starting to say 'I didn't invite' (you, presumably), which is a devastating callback to the Waitress being last resort
jokes.explanation: Good layering — the sponsor name becoming a live insult is a tidy callback. The 'I didn't invite' as a cut-off line implies the Waitress wasn't even wanted, which ties back to her earlier line about no one being free. Mid-tier execution.

dialogue.line: Frank's having a threesome in the bathroom with Gail and Artemis, and, um, yeah, I think the guys went to the Sixers game.

jokes.text: Dennis's monologue: 'Yet another reason why women can't compete with men. Besides your physical limitations, if given the opportunity to either work together as a team or tear each other apart, you will always choose the latter. Because women are devious and destructive and will always default to using their insidious venom on the most sought-after victim of all... each other.'
jokes.setup: Dee and the Waitress are fighting mid-match
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a pseudo-intellectual TED Talk on female nature — with complete sincerity — which is ironic because HE is the one who psychologically sabotaged Dee, making him the actual destructive agent
jokes.explanation: Peak Dennis Reynolds. The irony is thick and carefully constructed: Dennis is lecturing about women's destructiveness while having actively engineered the very situation he's describing. 'Insidious venom on the most sought-after victim of all... each other' is camp-level rhetoric that Dennis delivers with dead seriousness. The character integration is a 9 because this monologue could ONLY come from Dennis — his misogyny, his pseudo-intellectualism, his complete lack of self-awareness, and his love of a dramatic pause all converge perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Um... yeah, honestly? I don't give a shit about women's sports.

jokes.text: Okay, Dennis is right. / ...Because they're stupid.
jokes.setup: Dee pivots from the fight to agree with Dennis's monologue and proposes using 'mental manipulation'
jokes.punchline: The elaborate buildup to 'why?' is answered with the blunt, unadorned: '...Because they're stupid.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. The comedic construction is classic misdirection — the elaborate strategic pivot, the portentous 'Do you want to know why?' / 'Why?' exchange builds expectation for something clever, and the punchline is the most reductive possible answer. The beat before 'Because... they're stupid' sells it. This is excellent joke construction: maximum setup, minimum punchline words, maximum impact.

jokes.text: Hey Mac, how come you throw the ball so straight? / I throw the ball straight because, as a man, dominance is my sporting style. / Uh, I heard it's 'cause you have no finesse. You don't know how to spin the ball.
jokes.setup: The women's psychological manipulation plan is now in action — targeting Mac's ego
jokes.punchline: Mac's response to 'why do you throw it straight' is an immediate self-aggrandizing character statement about dominance — which is exactly the button they needed to push
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback to the opening 'finesse' joke — Mac's finesse weakness is now being weaponized. 'As a man, dominance is my sporting style' is a perfect Mac line that calls back to Dennis's 'dominate the table into submission.' The word 'finesse' landing as the exact vulnerability is a beautiful full-circle structural beat. The plan working is satisfying because the audience was given the information early.

jokes.text: Mac arguing with Dennis: 'She said that I can't spin, and I can spin.' / 'You... Do not try it.' / 'But Dennis, she said I have no finesse, and you know that I have finesse.' / 'Don't-don't do it.'
jokes.setup: Dennis can see Mac is about to be manipulated into spinning the ball
jokes.punchline: Mac is so desperate for validation of his finesse that he almost pleads with Dennis for permission to spin — 'Can I just spin one?' — the manipulation is working in real time
jokes.explanation: Good tension-building cringe. Mac's ego is being so perfectly exploited that he essentially asks permission to be an idiot. 'Can I just spin one?' with mounting desperation is excellent character work. The audience knows what's coming which creates satisfying dread.

jokes.text: Stride, stride, stride, SPIN!
jokes.setup: Mac promised Dennis he wouldn't spin; he approaches the lane reciting his mantra
jokes.punchline: The final word of his approach mantra changes from 'execute' to 'SPIN' — he has betrayed himself with the same verbal sabotage structure that Dennis uses on Dee
jokes.explanation: The best single joke in the episode. The structural perfection is extraordinary: Mac's approach mantra ('stride, stride, stride, execute') was introduced early, the finesse manipulation was set up meticulously, and the payoff is the mantra itself mutating — the EXACT moment Mac betrays his own plan is encoded in the word change. Everything converges: the finesse callback from the cold open, the mantra as a running gag, and Mac's ego as his fatal flaw. The delivery is pure comedy — 'execute' becoming 'SPIN' at the last instant shows Mac's character defeating his logic. Economy score is near-perfect: four words tell a complete arc. This is the kind of joke that gets quoted and replayed.

jokes.text: Oh, goddamn it! — gutter ball result
jokes.setup: Mac spins the ball despite being told not to
jokes.punchline: Gutter ball. Dennis's exasperated 'Oh, goddamn it!' is the audience surrogate reaction.
jokes.explanation: Functional button on the spin joke. Dennis's reaction is the right one and it lands as confirmation. The score reflects that this is a reaction beat rather than a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Hey, Tyrone, double or nothing! 'Cause there's no way you're beating me two out of three, dude!
jokes.setup: It's Charlie's turn to bowl; he's supposed to be helping the team
jokes.punchline: Charlie is gambling with a child at air hockey — he's so embedded in the birthday party that he's now wagering money against a kid
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation of the birthday party running gag. Charlie has gone from watching the party to actively competing in it to now GAMBLING with a child. The escalation is perfect Charlie logic. 'Double or nothing' with a birthday party kid is very specific and very funny.

jokes.text: The Waitress distracts Charlie by asking about his elbow technique — he demonstrates and rolls a gutter ball
jokes.setup: The women's manipulation plan targets Charlie; they compliment him as a 'good natural bowler'
jokes.punchline: Charlie, flattered, over-thinks his natural technique while demonstrating his elbow position and immediately loses it — a gutter ball from someone who was apparently a natural
jokes.explanation: Good psychological manipulation beat. The irony of asking someone to explain their natural unconscious skill — thus making them conscious of it and destroying it — is a real psychological phenomenon played for comedy. Charlie's sincerity in wanting to help is what sells it.

jokes.text: Gutter ball. Gutter ball. Stride, stride, stride, spin! Come on! Gutter ball. S-Stop it. Gutter ball. Come on. Gutter ball.
jokes.setup: Mac keeps attempting to spin the ball; keeps rolling gutter balls
jokes.punchline: Mac is now incapable of NOT saying 'spin' in his mantra — a montage of gutter balls with the mantra mutating each time, mirroring Dee's conditioned gutter ball response
jokes.explanation: The parallel structure is elegant — Mac is now conditioned to fail by his own ego just as Dee was conditioned by Dennis. The montage of gutter balls is good escalation comedy. Dennis's 'S-Stop it' is an excellent reaction. The thematic mirroring makes this smarter than a simple running gag.

jokes.text: In the third act of my play, Donna rolls a gutter ball in the big match against her rival high school.
jokes.setup: Artemis rolls a gutter ball mid-match
jokes.punchline: Artemis has not rolled a gutter ball — her character Donna has, in the THIRD ACT of a play Artemis has apparently been writing/performing this entire time
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Artemis moment and an excellent escalation of the Donna character. The revelation that this entire bowling match has been ACT THREE of a play — and that the gutter ball was a scripted dramatic beat — is a perfect absurdist payoff. The meta-layer (her character has a dramatic arc WITHIN the actual episode's plot) is clever writing. Character integration is a 9 because this is uniquely Artemis-brained thinking.

jokes.text: Now, technically, I could pick up this spare and push the lead even further, and I think we all know Dee's about to roll two gutter balls. So I'll tell you what. Dee, if you would like, you could just quit now and you could all admit that you're inferior in every single way.
jokes.setup: Dennis's team is ahead; Dee needs to perform in the final frame
jokes.punchline: Dennis offers to let Dee quit now and admit total inferiority — delivered with the condescending grace of a villain granting mercy
jokes.explanation: Very Dennis — the elegant cruelty of offering a 'mercy' that is actually just an opportunity to humiliate. 'Admit that you're inferior in every single way' is a nicely over-the-top demand. Good character moment building toward the climax.

jokes.text: Okay, you know what, dick? I don't like your sister. She's a terrible person. She's a bitch and she's ugly and I didn't want her on the team. And she's gross. Sure, and she's gross. But you know what? You're even worse. And I am not gonna sit here and let you just shit on her all night long.
jokes.setup: Dennis is demanding Dee quit; Dee needs to respond
jokes.punchline: Dee defends the Waitress by first thoroughly insulting her — 'she's a bitch and she's ugly and I didn't want her on the team, AND she's gross' — then pivoting to defending her honor. Dennis helpfully confirms 'and she's gross.'
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Sunny — the 'heroic speech' format is immediately subverted. Dee's attempt at a rousing defense of the Waitress begins with a comprehensive takedown of the Waitress. Dennis's unprompted 'Sure, and she's gross' agreement is a perfect bit. The structure of 'she's terrible BUT I'll defend her' is a great inversion of the usual emotional beat. Character-specific because only Dee would accidentally expose her contempt for someone while claiming to defend them.

jokes.text: Okay, you know what, dick? I don't like your sister. She's a terrible person. She's a bitch and she's ugly and I didn't want her on the team. And she's gross. / Sure, and she's gross. / But you know what? You're even worse.
jokes.setup: Dee tries to psychologically intimidate Dennis before she bowls.
jokes.punchline: Dee's big emotional stand involves first deeply insulting her own teammate (the Waitress) — 'terrible person, bitch, ugly, gross' — before getting to her actual point. Mac's casual 'sure, and she's gross' is a perfect agreement beat.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Dee's inspirational stand involves thoroughly trashing her own teammate before making a point about solidarity. It's perfectly in-character for how the gang operates, and Mac's 'sure, and she's gross' as a casual confirmation is excellent. The structure — insult teammates, then claim moral high ground — is very Always Sunny.

jokes.text: I summon the very fact that I am a man! — Dennis punches the high striker machine
jokes.setup: Dee challenges Dennis to a strength contest on the high striker machine; he accepts with theatrical bravado
jokes.punchline: 'I summon the very fact that I am a man!' — delivered as an incantation before hitting the machine, followed by presumably injuring his hand catastrophically
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode and an all-time Dennis Reynolds quote. 'I summon the very fact that I am a man' is extraordinary — it condenses his entire worldview (masculine superiority as a metaphysical force) into a single ritual incantation. The phrasing 'summon the very fact' is deliriously specific in a way that elevates it from a generic macho line to pure Dennis poetry. The immediate physical consequence (shattering his hand) punishes the hubris perfectly. This is the anchor that the episode builds toward thematically. Highly quotable, highly rewatch-able.

jokes.text: I've broken every single bone in my hand. I cannot bowl. There's nothing solid left in there. It's just bloody soup and bone broth.
jokes.setup: Dennis has just destroyed his hand on the high striker
jokes.punchline: 'Bloody soup and bone broth' — Dennis's clinical, culinary description of his destroyed hand is grotesque and funny
jokes.explanation: Exceptional line. 'Bloody soup and bone broth' is a culinary-grotesque description that is uniquely Dennis — his tendency to intellectualize and aestheticize even his own suffering. The specificity of 'bone broth' (a trendy food item, not just 'liquid') is perfect. This is a highly quotable, memorable line that works both as physical comedy and character revelation. Near-top tier for the episode.

jokes.text: Now, I need to scream. And I need you to find me somewhere to scream so I don't have to do it here. / No, wait a minute. I'm going to scream here, and now, 'cause I can't hold it in, so here we go.
jokes.setup: Dennis has destroyed his hand and needs to process the pain
jokes.punchline: Dennis formally announces he is about to scream, announces he needs a private location, then immediately contradicts himself and screams publicly — the structure of the announcement is funnier than any scream
jokes.explanation: Dennis treating his own emotional outburst as a formal procedure with location requirements is very Dennis. The immediate self-contradiction ('I'm going to scream here, and now, 'cause I can't hold it in') adds another layer of his failed self-control under the controlled exterior. 'So here we go' is a perfect button — almost polite.

jokes.text: Ryan, I need you to bowl for me. I'll never bowl again. / The story's too horrible to tell. / Oh, with this stuff.
jokes.setup: Dennis asks Ryan McPoyle to bowl for him; Ryan refuses citing his tragic accident
jokes.punchline: Ryan deploys Liam's 'story too horrible to tell' construction — the McPoyle verbal tic is now being recycled within the same episode
jokes.explanation: Third iteration of the 'story too horrible' gag — the McPoyle verbal tic has spread to both brothers. Mac's exasperated 'Oh, with this stuff' is a good audience-surrogate reaction. Sets up the eventual devastating reveal.

jokes.text: The McPoyle bowling accident story: 'There I was, practicing for the state semifinals. I was on my way to a perfect game. I was enjoying some chili cheese fries. They were delicious, and I offered some to Ryan. I accepted, but not realizing my other hand was in the ball return lane...'
jokes.setup: After multiple buildup moments, Liam finally tells the 'too horrible to tell' bowling accident story
jokes.punchline: The story is delivered with maximum dramatic gravitas — perfect game, chili cheese fries as the temptation, the fatal distraction — building to what should be a devastating injury
jokes.explanation: The long-form payoff for every McPoyle hint in the episode. The structure is meticulous: (1) the accident was set up 15 minutes ago with maximum mystery, (2) the chili cheese fries prohibition was itself explained as having a terrible story, and (3) the revelation connects both mysteries — the chili cheese fries directly caused the bowling accident. The cinematic pacing ('There I was...') and the dual-narrator structure (Liam and Ryan alternating lines) is excellent. This is the kind of long-form comedy architecture that IASIP does better than almost any other sitcom. Rewatch bonus is high.

jokes.text: It pinched it really bad. I had a nasty bruise for a week.
jokes.setup: The McPoyle bowling accident has been built up for the entire episode as 'too horrible to tell'
jokes.punchline: The catastrophic injury that derailed a career is... a bruise. A pinched finger. That lasted a week.
jokes.explanation: The best payoff in the episode and among the best long-form anti-climax gags in the show's history. The setup is extraordinary in its patience: four separate moments of buildup over 15+ minutes of runtime, each adding gravitas and mystery, all deflating to 'it pinched it really bad. I had a nasty bruise for a week.' The gap between the pomposity of the setup and the mundanity of the reveal is enormous, which is exactly what makes it work. The delivery of 'nasty bruise for a week' in the same grave tone as the entire setup is perfect deadpan. The chili cheese fries prohibition paying off as the cause of a mere bruise also retroactively makes THAT joke much funnier. This is the kind of extended misdirect that earns near-perfect marks.

jokes.text: That's it? / That's why you won't bowl? / You pinched your finger and you won't bowl? / Big deal, man.
jokes.setup: The gang receives the devastating non-reveal
jokes.punchline: Three separate expressions of disbelief at the extreme disproportion of a bruised finger causing a career-ending trauma
jokes.explanation: Necessary reaction beat that completes the anti-climax. The three-beat reaction ('That's it? / You won't bowl? / Big deal') is good structure even if individually unremarkable. The audience's disbelief is well-channeled through the gang.

jokes.text: O-Ow! Ow, I just, I just twisted my ankle. Yeah, and I need Ryan, I need Ryan to bowl for me.
jokes.setup: Dennis gets Liam to bowl for him; Mac immediately needs a substitution too
jokes.punchline: Mac fakes an ankle injury on the spot — transparently and immediately — to get Ryan to bowl for him, mirroring Dennis's legitimate injury with a completely fabricated one
jokes.explanation: Good beat — Mac's immediately transparent malingering mirrors Dennis's genuine injury in an absurd way. The fact that everyone can see through it and nobody says anything is a nice understated touch. Mid-tier but consistent.

jokes.text: O-Ow! Ow, I just, I just twisted my ankle. / No. / Yeah, and I need Ryan, I need Ryan to bowl for me. / No way. No way. / My ankle is hurt, and I need Ryan to bowl for me. / That... / That is bullshit.
jokes.setup: Dennis needed Liam to bowl for him (after his hand injury). Now Mac sees this and suddenly develops an ankle injury.
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately fakes an injury to get Ryan as his substitute — copying Dennis's strategy. The unconvincing 'ow, I just twisted my ankle' is transparently fake.
jokes.explanation: Mac immediately faking an injury to piggyback on Dennis's legitimate injury is classic gang behavior — opportunistic and transparent. 'That is bullshit' from Dennis (who has zero moral authority here) is the right response. Good escalation of the McPoyle bowling proxy situation.

jokes.text: This is incredibly weird.
jokes.setup: Both Dennis and Mac have brought in McPoyle brothers to bowl for them in this casual league match
jokes.punchline: Dee's flat 'this is incredibly weird' as the only response to this absurd situation
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — one flat line that acknowledges the absurdity without over-explaining it. Functions as a good breath beat before the McPoyle bowling sequence.

jokes.text: Ryan bowls and something goes catastrophically wrong — 'Ryan! Brother! Brother, what have I done?'
jokes.setup: Ryan McPoyle bowls for Mac; Liam watches
jokes.punchline: Liam's anguished cry 'Brother! Brother, what have I done?' — implying Ryan has been injured or killed by bowling, apparently because of Liam's interference — connecting to the original accident's themes
jokes.explanation: Excellent McPoyle payoff — the tragic accident motif is now repeating in real time. Liam's Shakespearean 'Brother! Brother, what have I done?' applied to a bowling accident is high camp that fits the McPoyle universe. The irony that forcing Ryan to bowl despite the original trauma leads to another accident is perfect circular logic. Rewatch bonus because on second viewing you can see this was telegraphed.

jokes.text: Oh, hi, Dee. I'm in here, too. — Dennis appears in Dee's internal visualization, joining the chorus of 'gutter ball' voices
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to bowl the decisive shot while fighting her conditioned gutter ball response in her own mind
jokes.punchline: During her internal visualization, Dennis appears — she has so thoroughly internalized his psychological abuse that he lives rent-free in her head during moments of pressure
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best conceptual jokes. The visualization sequence externalizes Dee's psychological damage — Dennis literally appears in her head, cheerfully announcing his presence. 'Oh, hi, Dee. I'm in here, too.' is a perfect line: casual, friendly, devastating. It crystallizes the Dennis/Dee relationship with more economy than any straight dialogue could. The meta-physical manifestation of childhood trauma as a mid-bowling visualization is exactly the kind of dark absurdism IASIP does uniquely well. High character integration because this speaks to their specific history.

jokes.text: Well, well, well, Dee, it looks like you're gonna have to roll after all. / Fine. No problem. Gonna make my team proud. / Oh, well, maybe you will. / Or maybe... you'll roll a gutter ball.
jokes.setup: With both McPoyle substitutes apparently out of commission, Dee must bowl to win.
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers 'or maybe... you'll roll a gutter ball' with full theatrical weight — the phrase that has broken Dee all episode, now deployed in the highest-stakes moment.
jokes.explanation: The final deployment of the gutter ball curse at maximum dramatic stakes. Dennis's theatrical pause before 'you'll roll a gutter ball' escalates the phrase into a dramatic villain moment. Good structure, good escalation.

jokes.text: Gutter ball. Gutter ball. Gutter ball. Gutter ball. — the chorus of voices in Dee's head, then the actual gutter balls as she rolls
jokes.setup: Dee's internal visualization is overwhelmed with 'gutter ball' voices; she bowls
jokes.punchline: She rolls multiple gutter balls in a row — the psychological conditioning is complete and total
jokes.explanation: Satisfying escalation of the gutter ball motif to its logical extreme — Dee can no longer bowl at all. The cumulative effect is good, though the individual jokes at this point are running on the gag's established momentum rather than fresh comedy.

jokes.text: Dee bowls a strike — 'I did it! In your faces!'
jokes.setup: Dee has rolled multiple gutter balls and seems defeated; the episode builds to her failure
jokes.punchline: She actually overcomes it — genuine triumph — which subverts the expected Dee-fails ending. 'In your faces!'
jokes.explanation: Good subversion of the expected Dee-always-loses ending. The genuine triumph is earned by the arc but undercut immediately by the final joke, which makes this a setup for the real punchline. Works well structurally as a fake-out before the deflation.

jokes.text: Ha... Uh... What's going on? / Frank's having a threesome in the bathroom with Gail and Artemis, and, um, yeah, I think the guys went to the Sixers game. / What? / Oh, goddamn it.
jokes.setup: Dee has just achieved her victory — everyone should be celebrating
jokes.punchline: Everyone has left. Frank is having a bathroom threesome. The guys went to a basketball game. Nobody cared about Dee's triumph.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Sunny ending. The show's core cynicism — no triumph matters if no one witnesses it — lands with great precision. 'Frank's having a threesome in the bathroom with Gail and Artemis' is both funny as a detail (of course Frank is) and a great Artemis callback (her character's whorishness was seeded). The deflation of Dee's moment by complete indifference is more devastating and funnier than any explicit mockery would be.

jokes.text: Um... yeah, honestly? I don't give a shit about women's sports. / Well...
jokes.setup: Dee wonders why the Waitress isn't celebrating their apparent win.
jokes.punchline: The Waitress admits she doesn't care about women's sports — which means the entire episode's competition was meaningless to even the people on Dee's side.
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing callback to the men's discussion that 'women don't even like women's sports.' The Waitress confirming this — from inside the women's team — is the darkly comic thesis statement. It retroactively validates the guys' (terrible) point while also proving it doesn't matter anyway. The 'Well...' from Dee as the final line, with no response, is the ideal ending. Excellent economy and structural callback.

jokes.text: Um... yeah, honestly? I don't give a shit about women's sports. / Well...
jokes.setup: The Waitress stayed behind — Dee assumes for solidarity
jokes.punchline: The Waitress is indifferent to the victory and to women's sports generally — the last possible source of validation has also checked out. Dee's 'Well...' into silence is the final deflation.
jokes.explanation: The perfect final joke. The Waitress staying behind implies she cares — but no, 'I don't give a shit about women's sports.' The callback to Dennis's misogynist argument being confirmed by a woman, without irony, is sharp. The fact that it comes from the most neutral party (the Waitress, who has no skin in the Dennis/Dee rivalry) makes it hit harder. Dee's 'Well...' trailing off into nothing is the ideal button — no rage, no protest, just quiet acceptance of irrelevance. Structurally it's the best ending note possible for this episode's themes.

tmdb_overview: The guys crash Dee's bowling league night and compete in a Battle of the Sexes at a bowling alley owned by the McPoyles. Dee, The Waitress, Artemis, and Gail the Snail versus Dennis, Mac, Charlie, and Frank in a classic match to prove who is better.
